utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ambassador, I would like us to have a soft landing and to go through some things as quickly as possible, because through your statements you gave me quite a few topics to deal with. Your journals are invaluable. The only problem is a lot of it is abbreviated, and then it can be interpreted this way and that way, whereas I would like us to come to the right interpretations together. Could we please try to deal with this now through yes-and-no answers as much as possible. I truly appreciate your inclination to defend the other side, but let us try to deal with this without resorting to tu quoque. What about your bosses, the heads of the European diplomacies and others; did they tell you that Mr. Izetbegovic could not be trusted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that ever arose. I can't recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution 065633. P780, actually. Page 61 in e-court. Do we have it now? The right-hand side, could we zoom in on the right-hand side, "Denis Pinheiro." The penultimate paragraph, "Denis Pinheiro." This is from your journal. It says: [In English] "Cutileiro was very concerned about what they see as Genscher’s efforts to lay all the blame on the Serbs and Milosevic for everything that goes wrong in B and H. Cutileiro says bluntly that Mr. Izetbegovic is a liar and cannot be trusted. Denis Pinheiro thinks it would be disastrous for the CSCE to de-recognise and expel Yugoslavia on the 29th of April. He is probably going to Yugoslavia, including B and H, before the CSCE April ..." And so on. [Interpretation] So it seems that they did report that to you, but it was an oversight on your part; isn't that right? I mean, is this not in your diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We heard comments along those lines about all of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's tu quoque, I think, Mr. Ambassador. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But say that to Mr. Tieger if he asks you about that. Now I'm asking you about Izetbegovic. None of them said that I was a liar. Could I please have page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please refrain from making comments. Put your question. Making comments does not help the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 62, on the right-hand side: [In English] "Bring pressure on all parties to calm down situation in B and H and tell Serbs and Croats to stop interfering. Tell the Muslims, especially Izetbegovic and Silajdzic, to work more with Cutileiro and stop running off to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states for money, weapons, and general support." [Interpretation] Do you agree that that's what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Ambassador, the accused made this statement like this in the course of his questioning. Let me find it again. Yes: "Now," the internationals, "none of them said that I was a liar," being Dr. Karadzic. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a comment. People did say that Dr. Karadzic did not tell the truth. Lord Carrington said that, and we had direct experience of it. The issue was not really tu quoque. As I mentioned right at the outset, none of the three parties in Bosnia was innocent. They all did very bad things. As we saw from the journals from the ICRC, from the UNHCR, things that were reported to us by actions on the ground, the overwhelming number of the bad things were done by the Bosnian Serb side, and I've said that. I don't have to say it again. In connection with the negotiations, specifically, that is, the attitude and the behaviour, we're quite used, as negotiators and as impartial mediators, to misstatements by one or the other side, to exaggerated statements by one or the other side. That's what makes negotiation difficult. There, again, are no angels. If I might give an example, I'm sure that Dr. Karadzic will welcome this. President Izetbegovic, in early March with the other leaders, signed a tentative agreement regarding a draft map for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some other items. When he returned to Sarajevo at the end of March, he withdrew his signature. No question about that. And this angered, naturally, the negotiators and clearly the other parties, but that's the kind of thing that happens in negotiations. It does not mean that this person or that person is inherently a liar. It's part of the game of negotiations, although it's not a game. But there's a good deal of back-and-forth on this as each party tries to enhance its own position. Thank you for giving me the chance to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Mr. Karadzic, see so refrain from making comments. Put questions. If you think that the witness lied, then put to the witness whether he lied, directly, instead of making comments. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, from the previous document, Mr. Ambassador, we see that Denis Pinheiro and Cutileiro say that the Serbs are being blamed unnecessarily and that it's somebody else who's a liar. With all due respect, Mr. Ambassador - now I'm dealing with your journals - nowhere in your journals does it say that Karadzic is a liar, but that kind of statement is made in respect of Izetbegovic in several places. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, Lord Carrington was the first person, probably, who told us that all sides lied, and that included the Bosnian Serb side. A leading Bosnian Muslim politician once characterised the three sides to me in the following fashion. He said the way to understand the fighting in Bosnia is as follows: The Serbs are butchers, the Croats are killers, and we Muslims are assassins. So even the parties, themselves, recognised that we were not dealing here with pure evil on one side and pure good on the other, but rather a mixture on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. We're going to show here the latest statement made two or three days ago, speaking of butchers, that it's not really the Serbs. Can I now have -- oh, I see, I see. It's already been admitted into evidence. I see. Now, can I remind you of yesterday's transcript. 75 is the page: [In English] "Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. However, that is not correct. You mentioned December 1992. That is exactly when it was published in the 'Jerusalem Post,' that there are more Serb refugees than Croat and Muslim refugees put together. Are you denying that?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "It's false, that's totally false and demonstrably false. We have the account from the ICRC. They took the refugees out. 'Jerusalem Post' is an English newspaper ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Could I now call up -- or, rather, do you stand by what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I now call up P784. The OTP 65 ter number is 06534.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you give the number again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P784 on page 35, the meeting in Zagreb on the 9th of September, 1992. So that was even before December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, Mr. Kumin: [In English] "Situation deteriorating in Serbia. Sanctions heard. Many Muslims going into Serbia. Serbian response to refugee inflow is a good one. On whole, non-discriminatory." Three points: "Needs to tell donor community that too much aid going to B and H and Croatia. It is needed in Serbia." [Interpretation] This is your diary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 36 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, who is Kumin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judith Kumin was at that time the leader of the UNHCR in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 36: [In English] "UNICEF - Lack of support from international community for refugees in Serbia." [Interpretation] That's also from your diary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask for P785, page 65, the meeting held on the 25th of September, 1992: [In English] "Mendiluce. Bosnian Serbs (and Muslims) also under pressure; either fleeing, fighting in Eastern Bosnia, or fleeing persecution by Muslims and Croats. "About 350.000 refugees now in Serbia and Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina. About 15 per cent Muslims. "Displaced Serbs in East B and H: 170.000. "Displaced in Western B and H: 150.000." [Interpretation] Does this add up to 320.000 expelled Serbs who had been moved out of their homes already in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest out-flux of Serbs came from Western Slavonia. The situation there was, after the Croatian, Serb, and Muslim attacks in June and July and August, the Serbs and the JNA continued to the hold Eastern Slavonia. That's the area of Croatia bordering directly on Serbia. In August, for example, they began the siege of Vukovar, which they destroyed, utterly destroyed. But in Western Slavonia, which is in the middle of the country, the Croatians rallied, defeated the JNA, and the Serbs -- the Croatian Serbs went south to Bosnia, which was Western Bosnia. That's how they got there. Now, excuse me, I should add it's one of the reasons why, when you see in my journal remarks by the ICRC and the UNHCR people about the Serb detention camps in Western Bosnia, Trnopolje, Omarska, Manjaca, really concentration camps, and they mention that the whole area is hostile, that even when the prisoners of the Bosnian Serbs are allowed out, they're in trouble, and the reason for that is that the area was largely populated by these people from Croatia, and it's to be expected that they were hostile. So that happened, and there's no question that the Serbs were expelled from Western Slavonia. And there's no argument that all the sides, leaving Croatia apart now, talking about Bosnia, that all the sides committed these kinds of acts. There's also no question that the overwhelming number was committed by the Bosnian Serbs, and we have quite accurate refugee count of the Bosnian Muslims who went largely to Croatia and then went all over Europe. Switzerland took in 100.000 or so. And, Dr. Karadzic, since you quoted my journal, could I quote you for a moment. During the Prlic case to which you referred yesterday -- excuse me, sorry. During the Krajisnik case, there was introduced into the record, and no objection was made, the minutes of a meeting between the Bosnian Serb leadership and the Serbian leadership at the Co-ordinating Committee in January 1993. I'm sure you'll remember that. And it was to discuss the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and this was the top leadership from Belgrade and from Pale and Banja Luka. And Dr. Karadzic is quoted, and here I have to be very careful, as saying -- really boasting about the following situation, and this is what he said: If you look at Zvornik, the city in Bosnia on the Drina, if you look at Zvornik, before the war it had 50.000 people evenly divided between Serbs and Muslims. Now it has 50.000 people, all Serbs. Well, what happened to the 50.000 Muslims? So Dr. Karadzic was not ashamed, was not worried, was not defensive about the ethnic cleansing carried out by the Bosnian Serbs, and this is a reality. I again repeat that all parties were guilty, to some degree, about mistreatment of civilians belonging to the other ethnicities. There was no question of that. Yesterday, I spoke about the fighting between the Croats -- the Bosnian Croats and the Muslims in the Lasva Valley, in Central Bosnia, so I think that's been established. And, indeed, we have many eye-witnesses to it. And, furthermore, that is precisely why these people have been brought to this Tribunal to be charged. After all, it is only a few doors away that the principal Croatian general, Gotovina, is on trial here at the Tribunal. Halilovic and Oric were tried here. So we all know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that they all did it. But the point I'm trying to make, and with which Dr. Karadzic disagrees, is that the overwhelming number of crimes of this nature, crimes against humanity, were committed by the Bosnian Serb side, in accordance, actually, again Dr. Karadzic, October 1991, when you left the old Bosnian Assembly, you said to them, If you vote for independence, it will take the Muslims on a path to hell. And that's just what you did. So you kept your word, you took them on the path to hell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador, for your kind explanation. I hope your points were taken, but I have to note that this is sort of a digression from the question. The question was whether there were 320.000 expelled Serbs who had been moved out of their homes already in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought I answered that by saying, yes, they came from Western Slavonia. They were not Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree that many Serbs from Western Slavonia fled in 1991. I also visited sports halls in Krajina, where the richest citizens of Croatia lay on floors, and that caused a great deal of fear among our people. Thank you for having reminded me of that. However, here a reference is made to Bosnia-Herzegovina. From Eastern Bosnia, 170.000 Serbs were expelled, and 190.000 Serbs from Eastern Bosnia. That's what's written here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Might I just point out that on the previous page, you will read: "About 200.000 additional Muslims still in Serb areas run risk of displacement." Indeed, they were displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll see in what way they were displaced and expelled. But, Mr. Ambassador, at that point in time they were still in Republika Srpska, whereas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, under the Croatian Muslim control at this point in time, that is to say, to the end of September, there was not a single village that was not destroyed and people expelled, where in Republika Srpska there were. And at that time, right up to 1994, in fact, many Muslims and Croats lived on, and the International Red Cross, in an organised way, tried to take them out of Bosnia, and I prevented them from doing so. And I have proof and evidence of that. Do you challenge that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from challenging it, Dr. Karadzic, that was one of the principal crimes of the Bosnian Serbs. Let me refer you to the August 26, 1992, speech of Dr. Sommaruga, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross. He mentions several detention camps in Western Bosnia as being particularly bad and holding upwards of hundreds of thousands of people. He mentions, by name, Trnopolje, Manjaca, and Omarska. Those were all camps run by your people, those were all Serb camps. Now, as I mentioned earlier, you offered to open up the camps. You will recall that. We haven't mentioned it yet, but at one point Dr. Karadzic offered to open up the camps, knowing full well that the surrounding population from Western Slavonia were very bad, and that was one of the reasons why the situation was complicated. The additional situation was complicated for the ICRC and the UNHCR was that the Bosnian Serbs, after much discussion, said to the ICRC and to the UNHCR, You can take the people out of these camps, the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats who were imprisoned. And this was a real moral dilemma, and you'll find many conversations in my journals to that effect. It was a moral dilemma for the ICRC and the UNHCR because, as they said to us, We will be co-operating in ethnic cleansing, and that, indeed, was the case. But they also finally reached the conclusion that it was a question of life or death for the prisoners being held by the Serbs, and so they did, in fact, take the prisoners from these camps into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. With all due respect, this is a rather sweeping statement and has to be established. Now, I'd like to call up Prosecution Exhibit 786 next, please. And what we claim all the time, Omarska and Keraterm were investigative centres where the state organs conducted investigations: 41 per cent were released, and 59 per cent of people were sent to Manjaca as prisoners of war, but we're going to show proof of that. But let's see what it says about Trnopolje in your diary, and the page is number 20 -- who was Thierry Germond, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was Thierry Germond?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thierry Germond was the principal delegate for Europe of the International Committee of the Red Cross and active in the former Yugoslavia; in charge of the Red Cross, the ICRC operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's see what it says on page 20 of this Prosecution Exhibit P786, or OTP 06536. On the left-hand side, Thierry Germond -- it says "Trnopolje": [In English] "Trnopolje, more than 1.000 people have entered the camp voluntary. The since it was empty a few days ago, that is the reality." [Interpretation] I say the following, and I have proof of that, which we might not be presenting during your testimony, but, anyway, we have them: Omarska and Keraterm were investigative centres where the state organs investigated more than 1.600 prisoners of war in speedy fashion, and Trnopolje was a centre where the Muslims, themselves -- well, they could come and go whenever they wished, and we have proof and evidence to show that. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned a few moments ago, the Serbs from Western Slavonia who had been evacuated to the western region were so hostile to the local population that the Muslims and the Croats were afraid, and some did, indeed, go into the camp at the end of the period, because going into the camp then meant that they would be evacuated under the auspices of the ICRC. So this is a question, Dr. Karadzic, largely of timing. There's no question that the camp was eventually emptied, or I should say closed and pretty much emptied, but the situation was very bad while it was open, and that's why President Sommaruga specifically referred to it to the world community at the London Conference in August 1992. Now, also, Dr. Karadzic, along this same line, you haven't mentioned but I will mention Tarcin Silo. Tarcin Silo was a prison camp run by the Muslims which had the Bosnian Serbs in it, and it was also visited by the ICRC. And we were told that the conditions there were very bad, about as bad as in the Serb camps. But I've said that, and I don't think I really need to repeat the point that all parties, in terms of quality, behaved badly. In terms of quantity, the Bosnian Serb side overwhelmingly was the biggest offender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to challenge that before this Trial Chamber during the entire trial. Thank you for remembering Tarcin. Do you agree that Tarcin, the Tarcin Silo, was closed only in the spring of 1996, that is to say, several months after peace was signed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned Zvornik and the meeting in Yugoslavia, I'm going to remind you that Mr. Vladislav Jovanovic was opposed to any forcible movement of the population and removal of the population; and I said, supporting Mr. Jovanovic, that that was a crime and that it was completely unnecessary because, in a natural way, people were moving anyway and fleeing anyway, and I repeated that several times at the Assembly sessions. And I'd now like to refer to one particular Assembly session of the 9th to the 11th of November, 1994. I think it's 65 ter document 00079. No, the 23rd of November. We need the meeting from the 9th to the 11th of November before that. The same session was held from the 9th to the 11th and the 23rd of November; 65 ter 00077 is the document number, or 00079. So 7, 8 and 9 are three pages of the transcript or documents. Here's what I said: "Never in history have we had a situation whereby war does not create a reality of some kind, and this war has done the same. The Serbs from Zenica are here now. Now, if you want to give the Muslims Zvornik, then you have to wage a new war to expel those Serbs back to Zenica. And it is according to that right that we are seeking Zvornik and a state of our own, and we will get it." So that, then, was an explanation on my part, not justification. It was an explanation. I did not justify the various phenomena that took place. I want to understand them. And they are my intellectual debates with you and with everybody else, all the international representatives, and not justifying something that took place and something that is stronger than me and which no power structures can harness.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your point of view, Dr. Karadzic. I have to say, briefly but forcefully, I disagree with it. There were not so many voluntary movements. There were, yes, voluntary movements, but the winning side always claims voluntary. The Israeli founding myth was that about half a million Palestinians voluntarily fled their homes in Palestine during the War of Independence in 1948. That's just not true. They were forced out. There are voluntary movements and there are forcible displacements, and the latter far exceed the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I don't believe that it was voluntary, but it was through people's own will, and the cause was the fear of a hostile environment. You mentioned that they were expelled from Western Slavonia because the inhabitants had this hostile attitude. Now, we prevented that, but what I'm doing here is defending state policy, and I'm also trying to understand the civil war and everything it entailed. I'd like to call up OTP document 11358 next, please, page 3, which is Lord Owen's book, "The Balkan Odyssey." Have we got that? Page 3, please, "The Balkan Odyssey." It's page 40 and 41 in the book. That's right. On the right-hand side, towards the bottom of the page, it says the following: "Once nationalism has found independent expression in Croatia and Slovenia ..." [In English] " ... he felt he had to establish Bosnia's independence from Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Izetbegovic knew that these would lead to bloodshed in this -- in his 'Islamic Declaration,' he warned that the Islamic renaissance cannot be imagined without people prepared for enormous personal and material sacrifice. "I have often wondered whether Izetbegovic might have found it easier to negotiate with the Serbs if he had not been a devote Muslim." [Interpretation] Do you know Lord Owen's position, as expressed here? Do you know that that was so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see, many of your colleagues, those who were at the head of these undertakings and those who assisted you, have completely different opinions to yours, and that is why I want to make a distinction between your explanations and what you actually saw and wrote. And do you agree that there is, indeed, a difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we call up the next document, which is -- no, I have a private question to ask you first. Are you a Republican or a Democrat?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, in the United States one does not ask anybody what's his religion and what's his party, so while I'd like to be co-operative, that is a question that we don't ask and we don't answer. I consider myself a centra-liberal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I expected an answer like that, but I know that diplomats as a whole, professional diplomats, career diplomats, are not affiliated in party terms. May we have 1D157, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you going to tender this bit of Lord Owen's book? It was already admitted, it was part of the evidence; 799, I was told. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope everything has been tendered so far. If not, we'll do so at the end of the session. But do we have the next document? 1D157 is the number. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's precisely why I asked you about your party affiliation. This is a Republican policy committee, and I'd like us to turn to page -- well, it says here: [In English] "Clinton approved Iranian arms transferred. Helped turn Bosnia into militant Islamic base. There is no question that getting arms into Bosnia was of great assistance in allowing the Iranians to dig and create good relations with the Bosnian government, a senior CIA officer told Congress in a classified deposition. And it is a thing we will live to regret, because when they blow up some Americans, as they no doubt will before this thing is over, it will be in part because the Iranians were able to have the time and context to establish themselves well in Bosnia: CIA alleged classified report says Izetbegovic has been co-opted, contradicting US public assertion." This is "Los Angeles Times." [Interpretation] 31st of December, 1996, is the date: [In English] "Izetbegovic is the Muslim president of Bosnia." [Interpretation] Tell me now, please, are you aware of this report by the Republican policy committee?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see it, but it doesn't have anything in it that is a surprise to me. I've already reported that President Tudjman on one occasion took Secretary Vance and me to the Zagreb Airport to look at an Iranian 747 jet plane, the big ones, that was loaded with arms and gas masks destined for the Bosnian Muslims. That was an open secret, that the Muslims, who were not armed, were trying to get arms from wherever they could. And we also have to bear in mind that the reason they were doing this was that since September of 1991, UN Security Council Resolution 713 established an arms embargo on all of Yugoslavia, so that the Muslims, who were under attack, had legally no way to defend themselves, which was anomalous situation, to say the least. And almost everybody we dealt with felt that lifting the embargo was the fair thing to do. Secretary Vance did not agree with that. He believed that lifting the embargo would widen the war, spread it over all of the ex-Yugoslavia, and he was quite specific in that. He was condemned for that position, but that didn't bother him because he believed it to be true, and I think it was true. President Tudjman, for example, believed it. President Gligorov of Macedonia believed it. But it was a complicated situation. I mean, here was a recognised government, after April 1992, in Sarajevo being shelled every day, 3.000 to 5.000 Bosnian Serb shells were falling on Sarajevo, and they were under an arms embargo. They couldn't get weapons legally to fight back. I think everybody knew that was anomalous situation, but the situation was so complex that nobody had an answer for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I like your documents very much, and the Muslims, I'm sure, will like your explanations, so we'll all be satisfied. Now, let's take a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's the kind of statement I referred to. Do not make statements. Put your question. Your statements lengthen the answers by the witness. Let's not waste your time. What is your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question was a yes-or-no question, whereas we received a tu quoque answer, which deserves a bit of humour, humorous comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next paragraph: [In English] "If you read President Izetbegovic's writings as I have, there is no doubt that he is an Islamic fundamentalist, says a senior Western diplomatic with long experience in the region. He is a very nice fundamentalist, but he's still a fundamentalist. This has not changed. His goal is to establish a Muslim state in Bosnia, and the Serbs and Croats understand this better than the rest of us." [Interpretation] Were you the diplomat with a great deal of experience in the region, or can you guess who said this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the diplomat, and I cannot guess who said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's a very arguable point. I mentioned at the very outset of my testimony with Mr. Tieger -- I outlined for you the war aims of all of the parties, and I mentioned that the last aim was open to question. Would they or would they not establish a Muslim state? Nobody knows the answer to that, because there were also very strong secularist tendencies inside the Muslim leadership. But there's no doubt that Izetbegovic was a religious man. And on that point, Dr. Karadzic, on the point of that Muslim declaration which you've read in extenso for the Court, we cannot forget that in February and March of 1992, when an expression of democratic will was called for by the Badinter Commission to determine whether or not Bosnia would seek independence, it was your party, the SDS, under your leadership and on your recommendation, that refused to take part in this democratic election. So I think it's a bit unfair not to mention those points when you also mention how non-democratic the Muslim declaration was. That was words; yours was an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. We'll come to that, all the points you raised. But the only problem is we can't challenge whether it says this in the document or not. We can't debate that, because that's what it says in the document; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Republican document you just read? It's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may we have 1D93 for a moment, and we'll come back to this document. But let's have 1D93, Mr. Ambassador, so you can see what deeds and acts are. Do you challenge the fact that -- and deny the fact that the Muslims procured weapons from Germany, and through Germany and Austria, including nuclear components?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any nuclear components being delivered, but there is no question that the Bosnian government did receive weapons, including from the United States. They landed largely at Tuzla Air Force Base. Everybody knew that. As I said a moment ago, it was an open secret, that people felt that the imposition of an arms embargo on a defenceless state was an immoral act, and therefore they broke the embargo. In terms of German weapons, most of those went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact is -- yes, thank you. They violated the embargo, and the reasons were other reasons, but the embargo was violated with the knowledge of the prime forces of the world and their governments. Now, would you look at this document, which is a document from the investigative organs from Munich. December 1998 is the date, whereas the indictment dates back to 1993. It says: [In English] "Investigative proceedings against Senad Sahinpasic, for arms," et cetera, et cetera. [Interpretation] So it's an indictment of the 9th of March, 1993. Now, they have we have "Explanation": [In English] "The defendant is accused of violating the Law on Arms, Law on War Arms Control and Law on Foreign Trade in 1992/1993 by shipping conventional weapons and procuring atomic parts and by procuring and delivering armament material to the Bosnian Army." [Interpretation] Is there any doubt with respect to these investigation organs of Germany and Austria?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's already been established that the arms embargo was widely violated, and, I repeat, it was an open secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that what they dealt with was words and that we dealt with actions. And you see that these are actions, actions aimed at procuring nuclear weapons, at that. 1D102, please, could I have that now. Excellency, can this be admitted into evidence; 1D93, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with first 157, the Republican committee report, and this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to 1D157, I have some difficulty understanding the relevance of a partisan -- clearly a partisan document, an attack by the Republican committee against a seated Democrat president. I'm not sure what the relevance is to our proceedings. Insofar as the rest of the document is concerned, it seems to be comprised of various newspaper clips that allegedly support that position. My understanding from the recent Bar table motion was that the Court was not receptive, or at least particularly receptive, to those documents for purposes other than perhaps some form of notice. So for those reasons, given the previous guidance by the Court and the tangential nature of the underlying nature of the document, I think I would have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to follow your objection as to the relevance of it. Probably, you are challenging the probative value of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the underlying document seems to be about Republicans attacking President Clinton. That's a bit far afield from the issues we're dealing with. The reason it's tendered, I believe, is because it contains allegations based on newspaper -- various newspaper accounts that support some of the propositions the accused is positing. But my understanding is that the Court has not been particularly receptive to such newspaper articles. If it is, that's -- I understand, and then the document has a basis, but the Prosecution will be submitting other newspaper articles that may well dispute those cited in this article -- or in this report, bearing in mind, in particular, that the report was prepared for a particular purpose; to attack the president's positions and marshal documentation that would support that particular view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, do you have anything to say? Would you like to reply to this submission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. First of all, I would not underestimate, by any means, the Republican committee, the political committee of the Republican Party. It certainly would not be showing off by providing false information and referring to significant French sources, like the prime minister, et cetera. I will be going back to this document yet again, so if that will make things easier for Mr. Tieger, you will see how relevant it is when I finish dealing with this document. I mean, really, if you can have hearsay arguments here and if they are not being challenged, and if what is being challenged is a document of the US Congress, I don't believe that, in the United States, any kind of congressional material can be declared irrelevant, any material related to either one of the two big parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds both documents relevant, albeit the probative value is a matter to be assessed at a later stage by the Chamber. Let's admit them both and then give the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1D157 will be Exhibit D79, and 1D93 will be Exhibit D80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed. Thank you for your patience, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have a word? Might I speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About this document, specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be very brief. Since you admitted it, it seems to me relevant to point out that the decision of the Court was to suspend the investigation, in other words, to stop it. They had information based on telephone wire-taps. It says that, but it also says that no documentation could be found. So what you have here in this document, with the word "Decision" at the top and then "Explanation," is a guess -- I would say an educated guess as to some actions based on wire-taps that were unproven. So while it's in the record, and I don't object to that, that's not my place to do so, but I think it's my place to point out that is a document of extremely dubious value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I have to say that the conclusion is not the way the ambassador had put it. The conclusion was that US law was not violated. I remember that full well. It was not stated that the arms embargo of the UN was not violated, so US law was not violated, and this was an elegant way to save President Clinton. However, I'd now like to have 102, and then we're going to go back to this document, 157, because it contains important statements made by important people, regardless to what extent they were taken into account, but there are quotations there of statements made by high-ranking UN officials and officials from other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see here that Hasan Cengic, who we know very well, and who was in power now, and who perhaps would not have been that dangerous if he were not in power, as you had put it, so he is providing information on the 2nd of February, 1994. He is informing his German partner, Mr. [Indiscernible]: [In English] "We are informing you and confirming that declaration whereby Amer Cviko is replacing Senad Sahinpasic in all transactions and mediations of goods. The document is valid as of today. Hasan Cengic." [Interpretation] Were aware of such activity in terms of procuring weapons, that there were indictments, investigations, dismissals, replacements, and so on? At that point in time, did you know that Germany and Austria were carrying out such large-scale investigations on the arming of Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, violations of the arms embargo, and even this dangerous access to nuclear weapons?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the point of nuclear weapons, as I mentioned in my previous answer, that was unproven. It's only mentioned in this document, which was suspended, and it's based on bugged telephone conversations with a criminal. As regards your question, was I aware that the arms embargo was being violated, the answer is, of course, yes. I've said that probably ten times this morning. And it was being violated openly. There's no doubt of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. However, I meant this reference to nuclear components, nuclear material, in the German document, not in the American one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have 175 again -- or, rather, 157 again, please. Excellency, can we have at number assigned to the previous document? Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is not objected to. Mr. Tieger, 102, Mr. Cengic's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Can we pass on that briefly, and let me just take a quick look at 102 again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's move on to D79.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the next page, and then under number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the page: [In English] "The radical Islamic character of the Sarajevo regime," page 8, "underlying the Clinton administration's misguided green light policy as a complete misreading of its main beneficiary, the Bosnian Muslim government of Alija Izetbegovic, rather than being the tolerant multi-ethnic democratic government it pretends to be, there is clear evidence that the ruling circle of the Izetbegovic party, the Party of Democratic Action, has long been guided by the principles of radical Islam. This Islamist orientation is illustrated by profiles of three important officials, including President Izetbegovic, himself, the progressive Islamisation of the Bosnian Army, including creation of native Bosnian Mujahedin units, credible claims that major atrocities against civilians in Sarajevo were staged for propaganda purpose by operatives of the Izetbegovic government, and suppression of enemies, both Muslim and non-Muslim."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to go back to page 3, I gather.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 3, you're right, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we're on the wrong page. Number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's paragraph number 3, the one that I just read out. You can see it here. That's the way it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of its provenance and the political party it came from, Ambassador, these are claims made by significant circles in American politics, that the regime in Sarajevo is Islamist and that it is committing crimes against civilians in Sarajevo in order to stage -- now, how do we say that? Yes, staging -- staging events for propaganda purposes. Is that what is written here? And do you think the Republican committee would lie with regard to this matter?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first question, it needs to be said, and we have to remind again this is a partisan document; Republicans attacking the Democrats. You can find everything like this today in Washington about the war in Afghanistan, the war in Iraq. This is normal American politics, to accuse your opponent of the most heinous crimes. With regard to the second question, would they lie in this matter, the answer is, yes, but they were probably misinformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't agree with that, if it's a partisan document, that that makes it false or less valuable. However, let's leave that to the American voters. They would certainly punish any political party that lied. Let us look at page 10 now, page 10 of this document. The paragraph is entitled "Sniping": [In English] "French peacekeeping troops in the United Nations unit trying to curtail Bosnian Serb sniping at civilians in Sarajevo have concluded that until mid-June some gun-fire also came from government soldiers deliberately shooting at their own civilians. After what is called a 'definitive' investigation, a French marine unit that patrols against snipers said it traced sniper fire to a building normally occupied by Bosnians."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "A senior French official said, 'We find it almost impossible to believe, but we are sure that it is true.'" [Interpretation] The reference here is "The New York Times" of the 8th of January, 1995: [In English] "Snipers shoot at civilians." [Interpretation] Should this be rejected as well, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. We've already discussed yesterday that it was Bosnian small-arms fire that killed some French peacekeepers, so this is not a contentious point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This has to do with killing one's own civilians in order to vilify the Serbs. Let's look at the next paragraph: [In English] "Breadline Massacre. United Nations officials and senior Western military officers believe some of the worst killings in Sarajevo, including the massacre of at least 16 people in the bread queue, were carried out by the city's mainly Muslim defenders, not Serb besiegers, as a propaganda ploy to win world sympathy and military intervention ... Classified reports of the UN force commander, General Satish Nambiar, concluded ... that Bosnian forces loyal to President Alija Izetbegovic may have detonated a bomb. 'We believe it was a command-detonated explosion, probably in a can' ..." [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, should this be taken seriously as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, this should be taken seriously. As we can read by the very language, it's not definitive. "May have detonated a bomb," quote, "may have -- Bosnian forces loyal to President Alija Izetbegovic may have detonated a bomb." Well, maybe they did, maybe they didn't. They're not accusing the government of a specific action. But we've already discussed yesterday, Dr. Karadzic, the point that I brought to your and to the Court's attention about the Bosnian Muslim Army firing from the grounds of the hospital in order to draw return fire, so I can assure you I was no abject defender of the Bosnian Muslim position. My job is to bring the facts before the Chamber. Wherever the evidence leads us, I am willing to go, which is why I mentioned that hospital incident. We would not be discussing this if I had not raised it. I don't mean that we wouldn't be discussing these specific points, but the hospital incident. But there was a good deal of confusion about who was shooting at whom. As we've said several times, it was a very complex war. It was not a two-sided war, side A, side B. It was at least a three-sided war as between the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Muslims, and the Bosnian Croats, and alliances shifted during the fighting. I think we've established that. I think we're all agreed on that. I don't think there's any argument on that. It's important to remember what I mentioned right at the beginning, that since the Muslim side was basically unarmed, that for most of the fighting between 1992 and 1995, about 80 per cent of the front-line on the Bosnian side was, in fact, manned by Croatian soldiers. And yet at the same time, while they were fighting against the Serbs, Mate Boban and Dr. Karadzic had a very important and quite friendly meeting in Graz, Austria, in May 1962 [sic]. So this was a complex situation. Their soldiers were shooting at each other while Dr. Karadzic and Mate Boban were chatting up in the Austrian mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you meant 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon? May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. With that, we'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We were dealing with document 157, page 10. I hope that we've completed that, and now I'd like to ask for page 11. Page 11, thank you: [In English] "The 1994 Markale market massacre": "French television reported last night that United Nations investigation into the market-place bombing in Sarajevo two weeks ago had established beyond doubt that the mortar shell that killed 68 people was fired from inside Bosnian (Muslim) lines." [Interpretation] That was published in "The Times" in 1994, on the 19th of February: [In English] "A senior UN official has admitted the existence of a secret UN report that blames the Bosnian Muslims for the February 1994 massacre of the Muslims at the Sarajevo market ... after studying the crater left by the mortar shell and the distribution of shrapnel, the report concluded that the shell was fired from behind Muslim lines." [Interpretation] Now, it says: [In English] "Policy": [Interpretation] On the 22nd of December, 1994, by David Binder: [In English] "A veteran 'New York Times' reporter in Yugoslavia had access to the suppressed report. Bodansky categorically stated that the bomb 'was actually a special charge designed and built with the help of Hezbollah Party (pro-Iranian terror group) expert and then most likely dropped from a nearby rooftop onto the crowd of shoppers. Video cameras at the ready recorded this expertly-staged spectacle in gore, which dozens of corpses of Bosnian Muslim troops killed in action (exchanged the day before in the body swap with the Serbs) were paraded in front of the cameras to raise the casualties count." [Interpretation] Does this change your position, Mr. Ambassador, about Serb misdeeds and specifically about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two questions, two answers. About these incidents, I was aware, although I was not actively involved at the time, of the differences of opinions as to the origin of the market massacre in 1994 and the 1995 incident. On the second point, does it change my opinion, I have to say, no, it does not. I mean, if I could just give an example of an incident in 1995, about the same time, that nobody has disputed - the evidence is overwhelming - namely, the Bosnian Serb Army's murder of 7.000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica. If Dr. Karadzic wants to raise that, I'd be interested to hear his views, but it's an unarguable fact that this happened. Again, just to be brief, all sides behaved badly. The Bosnian Serb side behaved worst of all. And since they had the better arms, because they had not only their own Bosnian Serb Army, they had the Yugoslav Army behind them, they were able to do more damage. But it is an unarguable fact, and we've established that, I think, here, Dr. Karadzic and I, that some blame attaches to all sides in wars like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Do you agree that this answer of yours makes it right for me to appreciate your writings and documents more than your opinions and assessments? Just give a yes-or-no answer. That will do.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not make you right to draw those conclusions because, unfortunately, they are not the correct conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my cue comes from you to speak about Srebrenica. However, we will get to that as well. Let's just quickly finish dealing with this document, the next paragraph, and then move on to other subjects: [In English] "The 1995 second market massacre": "A crucial UN report stating Serb responsibility for the market massacre is a classified secret, but for specialists - a Russian, a Canadian, and two Americans - have raised serious doubts about its conclusion, suggesting instead that the mortar was fired not by the Serbs, but by Muslim government forces. A Canadian officer added that he and fellow Canadian officers in Bosnia were convinced that the Muslim government dropped both the February 5, 1994, and the August 28, 1995, mortar shells on the Sarajevo markets. An unidentified US official contends that the available evidence suggests either the shell was fired at a very low trajectory, which means a range of a few hundred yards - therefore under the Sarajevo government control - or the mortar shell, converted into a bomb, was dropped from a nearby roof into the crowd." [Interpretation] That was published in "The Nation" on the 2nd of October, 1995. A bit further down: [In English] "French managing editor Jean Denir [phoen] put the question directly to Prime Minister Edouard Balladur, 'They,'" meaning Muslims, "'have committed this carnage on their own people.' I explained in consternation. 'Yes,' confirmed the prime minister without hesitation, 'but at least they have forced NATO to intervene.'" [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, do you have Prime Minister Balladur would be partial or would have any reason to present something that was not the truth?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're all agreed that violence was committed by all sides. It's one of the reasons, Dr. Karadzic, these incidents that you bring to our attention, it's one of the reasons why we implored with you the Serb shelling of Sarajevo. You'll recall Lord Owen said more than once that it was probably the single biggest item that harmed your side; namely, the daily shelling of an innocent city, which, by the way, one cannot forget, is, in itself, a war crime. I have to admit that even at this late date, I do not understand why you didn't order General Mladic to stop shelling Sarajevo and Gorazde and the other cities that you besieged. It surely did you harm with the rest of the world, and it is something of a mystery to me still, why you continued this shelling, knowing that it was bringing you this harm. Now, I'm aware of your argument - we discussed this - about 60.000 Serbs allegedly being held hostage in Sarajevo. Of course, you know that. But even so, I have to say that was actually not true, because after UNHCR took over the airport of Sarajevo in June/July 1992, there were relief flights and mercy flights taking people in and out. That was how the negotiators actually got in, on the UNHCR flights, and very few Serbs applied for those flights. But that takes us down a path that is of historical interest, and, of course, it's a charge that this Court will decide. But I have to say that I still do not understand why you didn't order General Mladic to pull his troops off Mount Igman or just to stop shelling Sarajevo and Gorazde. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. That's a separate issue, and evidence will be led, evidence of a very precise nature, in respect of that. Now let's go back to another stand of yours, and a stand taken by the Prosecution; namely, that I ruled out the possibility of living together with Muslims in Republika Srpska. We claimed that we did not want to live in an independent Bosnia under Bosnian domination. We always asserted, in all our speeches and in all our documents, that we did, indeed, have minorities. Now, you challenge that as well. Could I have OTP 65 ter 2. That is the session of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is when we walked out of Parliament and established our own assembly. Number 2, 65 ter 2, OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that document, Mr. Tieger, what's your position on 102?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic's letter is admitted, the number being what?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D81, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D81, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, these are the stenographic notes from that session, and may we have page 47 displayed, please. In English, it is page 24; 24 for the English, please. And may we just have the English version on our screens, please. Professor Koljevic, whom you met and whose English was far better than mine, I'm sure you'll agree, do you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yours is very good. His was somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic says: "But this assembly of ours, we're not creating it to hold back somebody else's right. That is not in the nature of the Serb being. I think that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could we check whether we're on the correct page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 24 of the English. I can't see the page number there, and I can't see Koljevic speaking, who was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. May we scroll down to the bottom of the page, please. Let's try page 22. I think that Professor Koljevic takes the floor there. Yes. Now let's find that passage. It begins -- let's go back to page 24, and it's the second paragraph from the top on page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2: "What we sought to do by this act ...": "But we are not establishing this assembly to prevent somebody else from having their rights. I don't think any Serb would be able to sign up to something like that. When this sort of thing is being done, then it's not done in public, as we have been doing things. And ever since olden times, when they would assemble around churches to discuss issues, the Serbs have always done things publicly." Do you have any objections or comments to make to what Mr. Koljevic says here?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now page 25, please, in English. Page 25. After: [In English] "Confusion caused by treachery is passing": "... we want to preserve a state that will bring political and state unity to the Serbian people and to all those who want to share the state with us on the basis of full equality." [Interpretation] So we want to preserve a state that will bring political and state unity to the Serbian people and to all those who want to share this state with us on the basis of full equality. So this is -- he's advocating for Yugoslavia there; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that these statements of yours, that "we want to preserve a state," that will bring political state unity to the Serbian people, is consistent with President Milosevic's and, I suspect, your desire for a Greater Serbia. And it is surely consistent with your comment to me, when we first met, that if the Bosnian Serb opstina were not allowed to remain in Yugoslavia, that there would be war. You, of course, recall saying that. And, indeed, you made it happen, because you did start a war. With respect to the point that Dr. Koljevic made about Nikola's point was about allowing minorities in the Bosnian Serb Republika Srpska, you misquoted me a bit there, Dr. Karadzic, because you said I challenged that. I didn't. What I said was your war aim was to make the Republika Srpska as Serb as you could. I didn't expect it to be 110 per cent Serb; and, indeed, during the trial of Krajisnik he pointed out that there would be certain reservations, he called them, like Indian reservations, inside Republika Srpska where Muslims could live. So there would be these Muslim exclaves in Republika Srpska, very small ones, and that was understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. But this is October 1991. There was no mention of Republika Srpska. This is Yugoslavia here at that time. Nobody mentions any Republika Srpska, and our priority was Yugoslavia; whereas Republika Srpska was a choice of necessity because we did not manage to keep Yugoslavia. And so it's not about minorities in Republika Srpska that's mentioned here, but the unity of the state of Yugoslavia and full equality for all those sharing that state. Do you agree with me that in October 1991, there's no mention of Republika Srpska at all?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I just said that you were talking about linking the Bosnian Serb opstinas to Yugoslavia in 1991. That's not a point at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ambassador, it's at this point that we're asking for Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia, and all those who want to remain in Yugoslavia to be able to do so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're certainly entitled to ask. On the other hand, the referendum that was held, unfortunately for you aside, voted for independence, and in a democratic vote the people voted not to remain in Yugoslavia. That doesn't mean you were wrong to argue that position. It doesn't mean they were wrong. There was a difference of opinion as between you, the Bosnian Serbs and the SDS, on the one hand, and the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, on the other side. We've discussed that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All that was later, and we'll come to that in due course, the illegality question and the referendum question and the unlawful decision. And I'll put that to the Chamber in due course. But now may we have OTP 65 ter 5, please, document 5. And I'd like to remind you, Mr. Ambassador, that Republika Srpska, or, rather, a separate republic of the Serb people, is mentioned for the first time only after the illegal government decision -- BH government decision to seek independence. But here we're still dealing with the month of October and the struggle to preserve Yugoslavia, and for equality within Yugoslavia, and by the same token, within Bosnia-Herzegovina. May we have page 13 displayed now, please, on document 5. Yes, 13 of the English, that's right: [In English] "The basic principal": [Interpretation] "The basic principle that we need to maintain in our activities is not to force the will of the Serbian people," et cetera. This is what Mr. Krajisnik says: "Everything we do must take into account the complex political conditions, and all decisions offered up must be based on the Constitution and the law and reflect the interests of the Serbian people and not at the expense of the other nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The basic principle that we need to maintain in our activities is not to force the will of the Serbian people on other nations. We have to respect the justified will of the Muslim and Croatian population ..." And then we come to the crux of the matter, the substance of this. Where is that? I can't find it. Yes: "The essence of our strivings is clear, a life together in a joint state." So that is the position taken by the president of the Joint Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, in a situation in which we were out-voted unlawfully and then went to form an assembly of the Serb people which could, as such, take part in the work of the Joint Assembly. And it wasn't only the SDS that was in the Assembly of the Serb People, but all the other Serb parties as well. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may we have OTP 65 ter document 7. Number 7, please, page 13 of the English. And the date is the 11th of December, 1991. Radovan Karadzic says here: "I see. When we're thinking about the situation properly and well, and when we project the future, regardless of what we -- regardless of staying in Yugoslavia, regardless of the fact that we are going to remain in Yugoslavia, because that was forecast, I see that Bosnia will not be able to be organised like all the other republics, ethnic republics, because it's a republic with three ethnic communities, national communities, and I would like us to move ahead and use this term 'three national communities.'" It's paragraph 5 or 6: "When we think things over, we plan the future." It's the middle paragraph. Now, do you agree, Ambassador, that I'm striving to have Bosnia remain in Yugoslavia, but that Bosnia should take on board the reality of three national communities in doing so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it has never been a point of contention in this Court, and certainly not between us, that you wanted to divide up the state into three states, that is, three states within one state. And this is what you called, in various ways, a composite state, a federal state, a confederal state, and other expressions that all meant the same thing; namely, three states within one state. That's never been argued, and that's exactly what the Croats wanted also. The people who did not want that were the Muslims, and the reason they didn't want it we've also discussed in the map that we looked at, where they were given this patch of land in the middle, based on the Sarajevo-Tuzla-Zenica-Travnik diamond, and the rest of the country basically would belong and be partitioned between you and Mate Boban. That was the issue, but nobody has argued that you did not want your own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I would like to remind you, and we'll come back to your map, that it was always envisaged that the Muslims would get at least 30 per cent of the most developed part of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they lived in the towns, they were concentrated in towns, whereas the Serbs were farmers living on a large surface area of land. Now, I'm asking you something else now. Is it clear that we are advocating political solutions here and solutions which would take into account the interests of all three national communities?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not clear. In fact, the opposite is clear. If the -- if we go back to the preceding page, the one that you showed us just before this one, you'll see Nikola Koljevic saying that, if I could find it, that "we have all the advantages."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's 65 ter 5, page 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And what he meant by saying "we have the advantages," which is another way of saying, We have the upper hand, was that you were already by this time in the winter of 1991/1992, well armed, you're paramilitaries and the SAOs were doing okay, and you had the JNA, the Yugoslav Army, which as you pointed out a few days ago was, by this time, a Serb army, and they were behind you, and so of course you had the advantages. If I could read exactly the words: "We shouldn't underestimate our advantages, expressed through realistic ratio of political forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we cannot renounce our rights for others." You were stronger on the ground, and everybody in your party and all observers knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, Mr. Ambassador, your explanations and interpretations of Mr. Koljevic's words are unacceptable. He was never a military man, so you cannot change the sense of his sentence, where it says "political advantages," to translate them as being military advantages. We didn't need the agreement of Croats and Muslims to remain in Yugoslavia, but they did need our agreement to step down from Yugoslavia. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before, Ambassador, you answer: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure there was something to answer. My objection was going to be we're having further commentary and argumentation, rather than putting questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, do you think you can answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is -- to the question, "They did need our agreement to step down from Yugoslavia. Wasn't that the case?" And the answer to that is, no, they did not need your agreement because you boycotted the referendum of February 29 and March 1, which gave you and your party the chance to express your views. You chose not to, and, therefore, they went forward. I should also mention here, for the benefit of the Court, that already before the referendum on Bosnian independence of February 29 - March 1, 1992, already in the first week of June, the Republika Srpska had declared its independence, so that the fait accompli that they were facing was your previous declaration of independence in January of 1992, and that is also a matter of historical record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I limited myself to saying that you erroneously interpreted the words of Mr. Koljevic and that he didn't have in mind any military advantage, but political advantage, because we were a constituent people and against our will there could be no secession for Bosnia-Herzegovina. But let's leave that to one side. You have your view, I have mine. Let's go on and look at page 14 of this same document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What document? 65 ter 7?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, the same document, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, there, at the very beginning, it says: "Whatever we do --" Paragraph 2: [In English] "Even the smallest --" [Interpretation] No, paragraph 1: [In English] "Perhaps these three national communities will have the three school system perhaps --" [Interpretation] And so on. So in the formulation of this recommendation, one should perhaps say that where the Serbs, because of out-voting, are not able to retain their civic, national, economic, and other rights, that the Serb Assembly recommends that they set up their own municipality. Now, was it explained to you, Mr. Ambassador, that we were striving for having large municipalities, with many inhabitants, could be transformed into two or three municipalities according to the will of the citizens, as is the case in many other instances, that they can -- and that they can set up those municipalities on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points, if I might mention. The text on line 19 of the English, there's an error. It says "June," where it should say "January." The declaration of independence by the self-appointed Republika Srpska was January 1992, not June. I mention that because it's important to know that it preceded the vote -- the referendum of the next month. Now, on this point, Dr. Karadzic, whether the municipalities should be enlarged and have control of their own affairs, it's interesting to read it here, because when that was given to you in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which had 10 provinces instead of 109 opstina, 10 provinces, with large powers devolving to the provinces, and three of those provinces were Serb-majority provinces and they would have had all the rights that you mention here, you rejected the plan. So I have to ask whether and how much credence we can put in these words, when, in a concrete case after the fighting, with the peace plan on the table, you rejected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, allow me to make some corrections. On the 9th of January, 1992, was when Republika Srpska was proclaimed, whereas on the 7th of April, independence was proclaimed for Republika Srpska, not January. Secondly, I mentioned here that the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 21st of December, which it did not have the right to do - that's not what a government does - it sought independence, asked for the European Community for independence. Now, we're talking about 1991 here, Mr. Ambassador. The Vance Plan was in 1993, after the war, after the death of the babies -- the 12 babies in Banja Luka because nobody could provide them with oxygen on time, so those are two different periods and plans. Now look at this: "Even the smallest municipality can have three municipalities if we so decide." It's on that same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, and I'm very reluctant to intervene, but the Court has repeated said -- noted the nature of cross-examination, and it's for asking questions, and the accused repeatedly uses it as an opportunity for introducing comments and arguments, and I would note that's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree, Mr. Tieger. Please concentrate on asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can ask a question, and that is this: Do you agree that the Republika Srpska was only proclaimed -- founded on the 9th of January, but not operational until the 27th of March, whereas independence was proclaimed in April, after Bosnia had gained independence, or, rather, there was a session simultaneously in Banja Luka of Republika Srpska; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you're playing with words. Excuse me. Let's look at the situation on January 8th, 1992. You have something called the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next day, you proclaim your independence, the existence of a separate unit. I think that meant what it meant at the time. We all understood it at the time. And I really think your interpretation now, the gloss you put on it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. We'll come to that. All I want to do is to establish the facts. But let's go back to this document: "Even the smallest municipality can have three municipalities if an agreement to that effect is reached." Now, do you agree, Mr. Ambassador, that when the Serb assemblies were formed, the Serb Assembly, for example, of Sanski Most municipality - let's take that as an example - that that meant and implied that it would be both a Muslim municipality and -- here in December 1991, it says that if the Croats have the necessary conditions and prerequisites, they can form their own municipality within the frameworks of the former municipality; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That formula was clearly unworkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, but thank you. May I have OTP 65 ter 04984. Could I please have page 3, SA025898. This is the agenda, and page 3 of that document, ending with "98," I guess that's the ERN number. So let us move two pages ahead in relation to the page we see now, page 3 in relation to this one. At the very top of that page -- I don't know whether we have it in English yet. It's paragraph 2, and then further on the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, so you have to move on to page 3: "The president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, reiterated the need to establish Serb municipalities, where Serbs are the minority, without the obligation of having this done in all municipalities." Do you understand, Mr. Ambassador, that when the Serbs say that they formed an assembly somewhere where they were a minority, it doesn't mean that they proclaimed the entire municipality to be a Serb municipality. But it's only that part of the municipality where the Serbs live that they call the Serb part, just like in Brussels, where you have Flemish or [indiscernible] neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially true, Dr. Karadzic. Let me complete that thought of yours for the Court. More than once, the Bosnian Serb leadership was asked about the Republika Srpska and about the Serbian opstinas or municipalities which joined it, and what were the criteria for joining. And the answer was that in an opstina where a majority of the Serb population voted in favour, that municipality became part of Republika Srpska. What that meant, and this we saw in reality, is that let us suppose that we have a municipality A and it has a population of 10.000; 5.000 Muslims, 3.000 Serbs, 2.000 Croats. So the 3.000 Serbs vote, and if 2.000 of the 3.000 vote in favour of joining Republika Srpska, it goes to Republika Srpska, but that's 2.000 out of 10.000. And so while it is correct to say that the majority of Serbs voted, it is not correct to say that the majority of the populous voted.
