And that was precisely one of the problems, because these documents that we're being shown here, which I'm seeing for the first time, and I appreciate that, are all leading up to the proclamation of the independence of Republika Srpska. These documents are from December 1991, by which time it was becoming pretty clear that Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to follow Croatia and Slovenia down the road of independence. And so here we see the Bosnian Serbs preparing themselves carefully to take their land out of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- out of the rule of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't mean they were going to physically move themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, do you agree that this session was held on the 11th of December, 1991; yes or no? At least we can have a yes-or-no answer in this case.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, Dr. Karadzic, I always say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of what the MPs are saying, and the speaker of the Assembly, is it not clear that what is envisaged is that Bosnia remains undivided, ensuring the equality of rights in all municipalities; any community can establish its municipality, there is no regions, there is no partition? That is the 11th of December. Is it not clear that what is envisaged here, that even the smallest municipality can be established and that no one should be separated in any way; yes or no? What you spoke of earlier on, that's different, but this is the session of the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question is, no, it is not clear, and the reason is - and you and I know this - that the SAOs, that is to say, the Bosnian Serb autonomous oblates, were already being formed, and Bosnian Serb paramilitaries were already being armed by the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm challenging all of that, Ambassador, but I want to ask you the following: If, in a municipality, 10 local communes, Serb local communes, decide to establish a municipality, and after the 21st of January -- sorry, December, they link themselves up to a Serb entity, are you saying that these 10 Serb local communes decided on behalf of the entire municipality or only on behalf of the Serb part of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying -- I am quoting Mr. Krajisnik, who said that these decisions by the Serbs were made and involved the entire municipality, not just at few streets in some town somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to challenge all of that. Well, actually, number 7 -- or, rather, number 5 has been admitted into evidence, 65 ter 5, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with those minutes. We have dealt with, so far, four documents, number 2 -- in terms of 65 ter number, number 257 and 4984.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we are admitting only those pages dealt with by the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I've indicated if that's what's tendered, of course, that's right. If the entirety of the session is tendered, I think that's appropriate too. I have no objection to either course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is a separate matter, procedural matter, but I'm concerned about admitting extensive pages, while having dealt with part of it. But these documents, I take it, will be used extensively during the course of examination-in-chief and in cross as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think, in particular, we're going to find the Assembly sessions referred to repeatedly by both parties, yes, and I don't think there's any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Karadzic, on this, or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection whatsoever to the admission of all the transcripts of all the sessions, regardless of whether they were public sessions or secret sessions, or, rather, ones closed to the public. Everything the Serbs did, we have no objection whatsoever. However, then they will be viewed in their entirety as well, won't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber needs to confer briefly on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Following the principle we have been adopting so far, we'll be admitting only those pages dealt with in the courtroom. So can we give the proper name so far, the 65 ter 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 2 will be Exhibit D82. 65 ter 5 will be Exhibit D83. 65 ter 7 will be D84. And 65 ter 04984 will be D85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes, I understand that 4984, in fact, should be 0006. I just want to make sure we're talking about the same document, but I've been advised that it was listed as such. We can move on, and we can check that with the Registrar later. I just wanted to note that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they can be sorted out. I noted that it is on page 7 -- I'm sorry, is a seven-page document. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now have OTP 65 ter 9, 0009, that is, and page 41 straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Ambassador, I would like to remind you that we've moved on to the 21st of December [Realtime transcript read in error "12th of October"] already, and this is one day after the government unlawfully, in our view, asked for a recognition, and all the Serb ministers were opposed to that and they left that session of the government. Now, we have page 40 -- it should say "the 21st of December, 1991" in the transcript. As you know, there is intensive activity going on. After the decisions made by one side, the other side - in this case, that is the Serb side - makes its own decisions. Page 41 in the English language, Karadzic's remarks: [In English] "Our proposal is that in achieving this goal, it is possible to realise territorial and individual autonomy. It is possible for the little Muslim enclaves surrounded by Serbian territory to have their own administration, so that no nation can exercise power over other nations. Nobody's sovereignty must be threatened or denied. "Sovereignty primarily means power, the ultimate power over oneself," that means not the others. [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, you mentioned that there would be some kind of ghettoes or enclaves. In this paragraph, I'm advocating a single Bosnia. However, whether 30.000 people or whatever, everyone can organise an administrative unit of their own, for instance. It was precisely then that the Swiss Canton Euro was established precisely on that principle, the most recent one. There is no reference to Republika Srpska here now. It is only Bosnia that is being referred to. Any unit can have its own administration; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we're seeing here is basically your position that you've maintained as long as I've known you; namely, that the Serbs should rule the Serbs and not be ruled by anybody else. I don't find that surprising, because that is a position you've taken consistently. That's why you created Republika Srpska. That's why you ethnically cleansed mostly the Muslims, but lots of Croats, out of it. That's not at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is totally at issue, but I'm not going to challenge that while you're here. However, I am going to challenge it successfully, Mr. Ambassador. Now I would like to ask for this to be admitted into evidence, this session, or, rather, the numbers -- number 9, OTP 65 ter 9, page 41, the words I quoted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D86.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'd like to call up OTP 06147. While we're waiting for the document and -- it's page 029641 -- I think it's page 7, actually. In e-court, it is page 107. Let me explain briefly what this is all about. This is a Joint Assembly meeting attended by Serb MPs on the 24th and 25th of January, before the decision on the referendum. So a decision is in the making as to whether the Serbs are going to take part in the referendum. In our view, the referendum is worthless without the participation of the Serbs. Also, it doesn't work numerically, because they could not have a two-third majority to vote in the referendum. And even from the voters that did vote in the referendum, there wasn't a two-third majority. Now let us see what the situation was, whether the conditions were created for voting in the referendum. Now we have Radovan Karadzic on page 107. In English, it's 103. In English, it's 103 in e-court. So that's it: "Not to impose anything on each other. We will not stop. We will work around the clock until we achieve such a state organisation and such form which all three nations will agree to, Croats, Serbs and Muslims. Then we will hold a referendum that can be finished in 15 days. Gentlemen, that is the only way in which we can avoid unwanted effect, so that people calm down, so that they start living normally, finally. Believe me, we have no influence over war or peace. Situations are often outside our control, and I and all of us can imagine what would happen if, God forbid, riots would start now or an inter-ethnic and religious war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can draw that on the board. Serbs would run away from Muslim areas, Muslims from Serb areas, Croats would go to their own areas. Along the way, there would be shooting, there would be destruction of towns, there would be bloodshed, and we would find ourselves exactly where we are now; Serbs in Serbian areas, Muslims in Muslim ones, Croats in Croat ones, but fully homogeneous. And what will we have to do? We would again have to sit down and agree and place three signatures. Without all three signatures, there is no solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of that speech of mine on the 24th and 25th of January, and this proposal of mine to speed up the transformation of Bosnia and to have a new organisation, a new administrative internal organisation, and to have the Serbs join in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that particular speech. We were aware, in a general fashion and sometimes in a specific fashion, of the Bosnian Serb position on the question of the independence referendum, the decision not to participate and the decision to form units of your own in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, your colleagues subsequently made many comments to the effect that it was a major mistake to consider Serb claims to be illegitimate. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The claim to establish your own state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, along with a Muslim state and a Croat state, was an illegitimate claim because we also knew that it would ally the Bosnian Croats and their Community of Herceg-Bosna with the Bosnian Serbs and their self-proclaimed Republika Srpska and would be the opening measures in a partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina between Serbs and Croats. This was not a theoretical proposition. It was not a matter of saying that each individual is sovereign in his own personality, that sort of thing. It was a reality of how a country would be ruled. And you have always been consistent, Dr. Karadzic, and I've said it since the first five minutes on the stand here, in wanting your own state within a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall remind you that it was my wish that we remain in Yugoslavia. But now I'm going to ask for page 104 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the problem, excuse me, Dr. Karadzic, was that Yugoslavia was ceasing to exist. So that, you know, it sounds perfectly reasonable to say you wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, except there was no Yugoslavia to remain in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Ambassador, Yugoslavia was a great deal more of a state than Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Yugoslavia existed a lot more than Bosnia did. According to Badinter's opinion, Bosnia was crumbling, there were three entities that were being formed. So was Bosnia ceasing to exist as well; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badinter's decision on the question of whether Yugoslavia existed was negative. His exact words were, It is a state in a "position de dissolution," a state in the process of dissolution. That was not my opinion; it was the Badinter Commission. I'm just repeating it for your benefit, because I know I've said it before, but it does have to be taken into account that as the state was dissolving, the Bosnian Serbs wanted to join what, in effect, was Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with all of that in due course. Please look at the middle of this page. My speech continues: "We think that Bosnia and Herzegovina can turn into Switzerland, we can organise it as a link between Serbia and Croatia. Without that and prior to that, everything is a catastrophe. "I was delighted with Mr. Cengic's proposal," Muhamed Cengic, that is, the deputy prime minister, not Hasan Cengic. "Let us go in this direction, let us make the decision, let us set a firm dead-line for the democratic transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that, 15 days later, let us hold a referendum. Whatever we agree to, it must be agreed in such a way that all three peoples have full freedom." Were you aware of my position, as well as that of Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of your position. It was consistent, and we were well aware of it. Namely, you wanted a state of your own, and that you and Mate Boban were discussing the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You say it here, only it's more polite -- I quote your words, Dr. Karadzic: "We think that Bosnia and Herzegovina can be Switzerland, we can organise it as a link between Serbia and Croatia ..." No mention of the Muslims, who happen to be the most numerous people in the state: "A link between Serbia and Croatia." Well, that was consistent, because we knew that you were interested in partitioning the state. So it's fully consistent with what we understood at the time. And, of course, it was -- it led to a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, please, let's stick to our timetable. I talked to Boban on the 6th of May about something different, about not resolving territorial issues by war. However, let's go back to this. We say here that Bosnia would be transformed not into three units, as you have been suggesting; rather, it will be transformed in the sense that ethnic communities can have their own administration. Switzerland does not have three constituent units. Wherever there are 30.000 people, they can have their own canton. That's the case of Switzerland. Is that the way it was? Or on the 25th of January, are you saying that the Serb side ruled out the possibility of a single Bosnia with several units within it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary, I've said consistently, and you agree, that you wanted three states within one state. But with regard to your previous question about the decentralised nature of the state, and the opstinas, and how people should be able to rule themselves, when you were offered that in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, you rejected it. It would be interesting to know why, Dr. Karadzic. You had in front of you what you were asking for, and you rejected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, that was after a year of war, and I'm sure you'll agree with that. Now, Your Excellency, I'd like to tender the previous document into evidence, including what it says on page 103 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit this page of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll have a half-an-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I'd like to call up on e-court number OTP 65 ter 17, and the page in English is 5. No, sorry, 10, page 10 in English. It starts with: "Members of minorities ...," that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And before that, Mr. Ambassador, let me clear up one matter. It's my duty to put this to you, to avoid confusion over time. We're dealing with the 25th of February, 1992, here. That's the date. Now, it was just pending the referendum, but the Conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina, within the frameworks of the Carrington Conference on Yugoslavia, and under the chairmanship of Ambassador Cutileiro, was ongoing. Now, I want to do ask you this: What date do you put to the cessation of this conference and the start of your conference? The 25th or 6th of August, 1992, would that be the date?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date would be the conclusion of the London Conference, which was at the very end of August. I don't have the date in my head. Probably the 28th or 29th, something like that. And the beginning of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, the one co-chaired by Vance and Owen for the UN and the EC, was a few days later. I believe we arrived in Geneva on September 2. So the end of the London Conference ended Lord Carrington's operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is the 25th of February that we're dealing with now, and in English -- yes, we have that page in English, the paragraph begins with "Members," in the middle paragraph: "Members of minorities in a constituent unit would be protected in a way similar to that envisaged in Article 3, paragraph 3, of the Draft Agreement (The Hague document for Yugoslavia). And this implies absolute freedom of movement, includes total freedom of movement, which means moving from one constituent unit and taking up residence in another. In other words, major relocations from one unit to another without a special permit and not foreseen, as that would upset the national mix." Now, there, Mr. Ambassador, I am tabling a report to our Assembly, telling them how far we have come at the conference under the chairmanship of Mr. -- or, rather, Ambassador Cutileiro. Did you know that this was put to our Assembly and adopted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber had the opportunity to reconsider the issue of admission of these kind of contemporaneous record, given that they are minutes of the assemblies, and, as such, they are relevant and of probative value. And if both parties agree, for convenience and everything, we are minded to admit it in its entirety. What do you think about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's quite appropriate for a number of reasons, Your Honour, including knowing -- understanding different references at different points by different witnesses. I think we'll find it much more suitable, so I quite agree and think they should be tendered in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to emphasise that this practice is limited to these kind of contemporaneous records, not to books or et cetera. So this will be admitted in its entirety. As well, on the same token, the 65 ter number is Exhibit D82, 83, 84, 85, 86, will be admitted in their entirety. What is this number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 10 will be Exhibit D88, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it should be 17. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I stand corrected. 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D88, Exhibit D88. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to call up OTP 65 ter 18 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that, Mr. Ambassador, is the 28th of February. That means the next Assembly session. And while we're waiting for that to come up on our screens, let me say that in the space of three days, there was a lot of activity in the Parliament, in the Assembly. May we have page 8 displayed, please, page 8 of the English: [In English] "The chair said ..." [Interpretation] In the middle paragraph: "The chair said," and the chair was Momcilo Krajisnik, "said that the aim was that in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina no one should feel their status is different in a subjugated status. We do not wish to rule over anybody. Nobody who lives with us -- they should be treated equally," that's what it says. Now, two or three lines down, it says: "All three peoples, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, and there will be certain minority peoples. In Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, it will be others, and among the Muslims, the Serbs will be a minority. "That is why we must formulate it in such a way as to avoid making a mistake and putting somebody in a second-rate position."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this concept about the protection of minorities, was that something you were aware of, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender this? I'd like to tender this number 18 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D89.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up OTP 65 ter 20 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, let me inform you, Mr. Ambassador, that this is my report -- my reporting to the Assembly after full agreement was reached by the three sides about the Lisbon Agreement, or the Cutileiro Plan, as we referred to it at times. So we went on until early in the morning, and then that same day I reported to the Assembly, and all the negotiators did too. We reported to the Assembly about what had been achieved and what we had agreed, and we asked for the Assembly's support to have it adopted. Now, I'd like to turn to page 9 in the English. All we need is the English version, page 9, on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The institutions will proportionally --": [Interpretation] "The institutions will proportionately reflect the composition, and we do agree that they do so in the constituent units. If we have 6 per cent Croats in our units, then there should be 6 per cent of Croats in the police, the national guards, the judiciary, et cetera, just as there should be 12 per cent of Serbs outside our unit." Are you familiar with this proportionate representation, which was the position we advocated? Were you aware of that, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it. I was not aware of this particular document that you're showing now. I might add that the Cutileiro Plan, as it was called, was well known to us, and we discussed it at length and on numerous occasions with Ambassador Cutileiro, and it was acceptable to the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs, above all, because it established three states within a state. As we saw in the previous document that Dr. Karadzic had us read, Krajisnik refers to the three units as republics, three states, three republics, and that indicates pretty clearly that, in his mind, each one was, in fact, going to be independent. And that is the reason why the Bosnian Muslims didn't care for that plan, because they knew that they would be squeezed both between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs and that they would be squeezed out by the two larger parties. We've covered this extensively, I don't think we have to go into it, but it does explain the concern that the Bosnian government had with the Cutileiro Plan, and it does explain the acceptance, nay the joyful acceptance, of the partition by the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The evidence will show something quite different, Mr. Ambassador, in due course. But just another small question. Here I'm asking whether the agreement envisages everybody staying where they are and that there would be no population exchange or abolishing the existing minorities; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, another small question. Did you know, Mr. Ambassador, that the number-one personage who mentioned the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was Alija Izetbegovic, and this was well known to Zulfikarpasic, and we have enough documents to bear that out? But just let me ask you whether you're aware of that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I am aware of the Cvjetkovic-Macek plan which in August 1939 was decided upon between the Serbs and the Croats, and it envisaged the partition, the map was drawn. And I think 1939 comes before anything that Alija Izetbegovic ever said about partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'd have to say that three states were envisaged and proposed by Ambassador Cutileiro. But let's now focus on page 16 in the English. May we have page 16 displayed, please. And the paragraph I'd like to look at begins with: "We shall ..." And I continue: "We shall now have to establish a full structure of government on the ground, because this is our duty to the people who live there, Serbs, Muslims, or Croats, so that we can ensure peace. Then, through negotiations, we shall try to achieve the maximum requirements ..." Did you know of that position taken by the Serb side, that as soon as it is determined what our unit is, that we would establish peace and security for all three national entities, communities; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we knew this. But the whole point, Dr. Karadzic, and I must reiterate this, is that partitioning up -- dividing up Bosnia was never accepted by the international community until much later. It was later, but at this time it was not acceptable. So all of the points that you make about how the country was to be divided up were considered illegitimate, since nobody wanted the country to be divided up except you and the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Except for the majority in Bosnia; is that what you want to say? Isn't it true that this is Cutileiro's plan, proposed by him on behalf of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no argument about that. As I've mentioned earlier, the Cutileiro Plan, which you, of course, approved, envisaged three states within one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another small question: Do you remember that the Muslim side, with jubilation, stated that it was -- on the 19th of March, that it was happiest because the fewest Muslims would stay with the Serbs and Croats and that they accept the plan, and that it was only after the intervention by Ambassador Zimmermann that the Muslim side withdrew its agreement; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already discussed and I have already mentioned the fact that Izetbegovic withdrew his signature from the draft plan at the very end of March 1992, when he returned to Sarajevo from the discussions. Your remark about Ambassador Zimmerman has been denied, formally and under oath, more than once by Ambassador Zimmermann, so I can't accept that, and nobody else accepts it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the same document, but page 45 now displayed in English, please. Page 49 begins as follows: "We shall --" or, rather: "I think --" "I think --" The third paragraph from the bottom: "I think that the Council of Ministers --" [In English] I think the Council of Ministers will have to work around the clock to be able to prepare some additional laws, establish the SDK," this is a payment agency, "and so forth." [Interpretation] Then it goes on to say: "We shall announce our withdrawal from MUP, not to mention that we have already obtained badges. Our police will have to act in accordance with the law. No one -- not the hair of anybody's head must be harmed, regardless of their religion and nation. Everybody must feel absolutely safe." Now, do you see, Mr. Ambassador, that from the agreements reached, on the 18th of March we proceeded to have the Council of Ministers finish its job, and that we said that our police would be established, which we had a right to do under the agreement offered up to us by the European Community by Ambassador Cutileiro; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already agreed, Dr. Karadzic, you and I, that you were delighted with the Cutileiro Plan because it partitioned Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I won't pursue the matter. But the Muslims were even more delighted, and we're going to show that here, but we don't have time now. But staying with page 45 now, I'd like you to focus on the last paragraph: "That is why I ask you to do whatever is necessary on the ground to establish the de facto situation based on justice and the law, to have good and complete control of our destinies and territories, with full respect for the citizens of other nationalities. That is what people will be judged by." Now, since you have confirmed that, I'd just like to put this to you: Does this mean that we were ready to have minorities and that those minorities would be protected, and, of course, all this is happening on the 18th of March within the frameworks of the agreement reached to avoid a war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since it never actually happened, all one can say is that it might have happened and it might not have happened. I mean, it's entirely hypothetical, the point you're making, and I can understand that. But it is impossible to give a definitive answer to a hypothetical question that, in fact, never ensued in reality, because already by this time the fighting had started, by the middle of March, and by the end -- by the end of March, your army was already moving its artillery onto the hills around Sarajevo in preparation for the shelling of Sarajevo which began in early April. So it's a bit hard to -- I realise it's a little difficult to take these words off the paper and deal with the existing realities in Bosnia, but the reality was quite different from these words, unfortunately for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I like far more the "but," I liked what you said before the "but" rather than what you said after the "but." But may we have 1D75, please, which is Mr. Cutileiro's map to which we agreed. And it shows, Mr. Ambassador, that we accepted the external borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we also accepted the existence of administrative units within Bosnia-Herzegovina, without any territorial continuity, and that we also accepted that what you denoted as Eastern Bosnia should be in the Muslim administrative unit. May we have the map displayed now, please. Have we got the map? 1D675 is the number. I see we have to place it on the overhead projector. I think it's in e-court under the number 675. Yes, here it is. We have it on our screens. Now, Mr. Ambassador, this is the map we had agreed to, that we accepted along with the possibility of making slight corrections. Now, do you see that all three ethnic communities, national communities, have their administrative units which don't have territorial continuity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm well aware of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see where it says "Srebrenica," "Zepa," "Gorazde," that we agreed that this be within the Muslim unit?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, was this plan, in its different versions, the basis for all other plans up to the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did all these plans envisage administrative units? One envisaged three, another envisaged ten, the third one envisaged three, and the fourth one envisaged three as well, and the Dayton Agreement envisaged three; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Dayton Agreement envisaged and contains not three, but two. One is called the Federation of Croats and Muslims. The other is called Republika Srpska. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to your direct question, where the concept of three states within a state -- or two states within a state, was that envisaged by future negotiators, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Excellency, could this map, this very well-known map, be admitted into evidence? Now, Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll first admit the previous one, 65 ter 20.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 20 will be Exhibit D90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it there would be no objection to this Cutileiro map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think based on discussion, this map will come in as no objection. In that sense, Your Honour, I'm not sure of the precise provenance of this particular map. There is a map which the Prosecution has on its exhibit list, which is appended to something provided by Ambassador Cutileiro, which doesn't look like this, although it does seem to be -- it's not in colour. I haven't compared this precisely, whether this is a coloured depiction of the same thing. In any event, I don't have any objection to this map going into evidence. But to the extent it's characterised as the Cutileiro map, I'm not in a position to verify that, especially in light of the information I just provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. With that caveat and with the confirmation from Ambassador Okun, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A point that should be said about the map that is relevant, it was never completely accepted. It was always a draft map. And Cutileiro, when he presented it, said, This is for further discussion. So what we're looking at is a draft map, not a definitive version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just another small matter by way of a reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, on Friday the distinguished Mr. Tieger proposed an exhibit from my press conference in Geneva. Mr. Tieger highlighted the second or the third paragraph. However, the first paragraph of that document says Mr. Darwin has passed away. I expressed my condolences, and I say that we are going to remember him as the first creator of a map of Republika Srpska, and for that we pay our due respects to him. If we find that document, we will show this to you, but we are not challenging that it was Mr. Darwin who was the author of this first map of Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely correct. This map was routinely referred to as "Darwin's map."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm, Mr. Ambassador, that all maps were open to further adjustment on the basis of agreement reached by all three sides, three parties, including the contact group, all the maps all the way up to Dayton? Even after Dayton, we exchanged certain villages and territories; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question is: Were all maps open to further adjustment on the basis of agreement? The answer is yes. Quite obviously, until and unless the three sides agreed on a map, the fighting was going to continue endlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now I'd like us to have OTP 65 ter 28. While we are waiting for that, I would like to remind you, Mr. Ambassador, that the Muslims had accepted this agreement and also conditionally the Owen-Stoltenberg map, on the condition that they receive an additional 3 per cent of the territory, and that they signed on the 16th of September, 1993, Izetbegovic and Krajisnik, that is, that the Republika Srpska had the right to a referendum, including secession. Do you agree to that? We have that document.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm aware of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, which was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have page 87, 87 and 88 in English. Let's just check the English page, actually. 86, it is actually 86 in English. Radovan Karadzic, speaking on the 25th and 26th of July, 1992 -- that is to say, the war is still going on, but the Carrington Conference is still underway, until it was replaced by the Vance-Owen Conference, as we've agreed. The last paragraph on this page -- let's see whether we have the right page. 86, right. It's not on that page: [In English] "In the state --" [Interpretation] "In the state that we are building, we have to ensure that they have all the rights that we have, under the condition that they are not hostile towards us and that they drop their weapons. The villages in Romanija should drop their weapons like those who lived in Bijeljina and other villages did. The main condition is that they drop all weapons in order to be able to enjoy all rights." I have to say that the translation is imprecise. [In English] "Should leave their weapons ..." [Interpretation] Instead of saying -- [In English] "Some villages in Romanija are leaving their weapons." [Interpretation] So, Ambassador, the war is still underway. It's still the first Carrington-Cutileiro conference that is underway as well. And the position that we are taking is that we are going to ensure fall equality of rights on the condition that we are not being shot at. And I'm saying specifically that there are villages in Romanija that had already surrendered their weapons, and that they are living in peace like those in Bijeljina. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was also aware, since this is July 1992, that Arkan and his Serb paramilitaries had already started ethnic cleansing in Bijeljina. Milosevic admitted that to us. We've discussed it earlier, that Arkan was there with his paramilitaries. So while you were expressing these noble sentiments, the Bosnian Muslims were being ethnically cleansed from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the time being now, because of the "but" -- I keep telling you, whenever you insert that "but," you give me a lot more work. Let us move on to another topic. Ambassador, do you agree that Arkan was in Bijeljina on the 1st and 2nd of April, while Yugoslavia still existed, that is to say, before Bosnia-Herzegovina declared independence, and already on the 3rd and 4th of April, Arkan was no longer in Bijeljina? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because what you've just said, Dr. Karadzic, is not correct. He was, indeed, there with his paramilitary troops, but the statement that Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist is not true, because by April Bosnia-Herzegovina, as we know and we've said endlessly here, had already declared its independence, and, by April 7, had been admit into the United Nations and had been recognised by the European Community and by the United States. So it was a recognised state no later than April 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you've said just now that it was admitted into the United Nations along such a fast track that it was unprecedented. I agree with that. Mr. Ambassador, I did not say it did not exist at all. I said that on the 1st and 2nd of April, Yugoslavia still existed, and Bosnia-Herzegovina was within that Yugoslavia, and Republika Srpska did not function. It was the authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in Bijeljina, isn't that right, until the Republika Srpska started functioning on the 7th of April; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this time, Yugoslavia was disintegrating rapidly. Indeed, the very next month the name of the country was changed, as we all know, from the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia to the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Anyway, the army was changed, institutional names were changed to take account of the reality, namely, that Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Croatia were no longer part of Yugoslavia. But that's a technical matter, although it's a very important matter. More important is what was happening on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April, and what was happening was very unfortunate. The displacement and the ethnic cleansing, particularly of the Muslim community, was already well underway at the hands of both the Yugoslav Army and the Bosnian Serb armed forces and paramilitaries. I know, Dr. Karadzic, that this is hard for you to hear, but it is the truth, and we both know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That sounds like a judgement, rather than like testimony, Mr. Ambassador. I denied that, I challenged that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I would like to have 1D934 called up. And could the previous document from the Assembly be admitted into evidence, although we will go back to some paragraphs later if there is enough time. However, since you will admit the entire document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D92, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D194, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Ambassador, let me remind you that I took office on the 12th of May, and already on the 13th of May, and on the 13th of June, on behalf of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, I made the following decision, on the 12th of May orally and on the 13th of May in writing. The English version is not exactly legible. However, I'm going to read it. So this is the decision of the Presidency on the ban to establish armed groups and individuals in the territory of the republic that are not under the single command of the army or the police. What is also banned is the establishment and the activity of all self-organised groups and individuals in the territory of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Existing groups and individuals are duty-bound to place themselves under the single command of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within three days or the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina renounces groups that would continue to operate independently and will order the sanctioning of their existence -- the punishment of their existence and activity. Re-subordination to the single command of the army or police also means strict observance of the provisions of International Law of War. Were you aware of this order of mine, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to -- back to one of the answers that you gave, or, rather, it's something that you wrote down in your diary. What you wrote down was that I had said that I controlled the Army of Republika Srpska and 95 per cent of the paramilitaries. Now, what I'd like to put to you is a different interpretation: that I re-subordinated -- I ordered the re-subordination of all independent groups to the army, and that my only control was through the army rather than along parallel lines, lines parallel to that of the army. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course -- of course you preferred to control 95 per cent, and 5 per cent was either out of your control or perhaps just lesser. In that same conversation, you said that you were the commander, that you controlled the army. And when we asked you about General Mladic, you said, and I quote, He's obedient. So from that, one can conclude that when General Mladic led his troops onto the mountains around Sarajevo and started shelling the city -- or perhaps I should say should we conclude that he was doing that on your direct order? Since you said he was obedient, and there's no argument about his troops shelling Sarajevo, that was easily visible, and we had observers there, I think perhaps you might want to comment to the Court on that, but that's your decision, of course. But to the point, none of the leaders liked the paramilitaries because, you know, they're all difficult to command. Tudjman didn't, Milosevic really didn't, and neither did Dr. Karadzic, and I think that's understandable. But the reality was that the combat activities of the Bosnian Serb Army, the VRS, were under your control, as you so stated to us, and I think we have to bear that in mind when we discuss irregular or paramilitary activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. My question was whether I had some parallel units, apart from the regular army, and I think that you accepted that I controlled them because I ordered their re-subordination to the single command of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were already doing the army's business, so it was to be expected that they would become officially subordinated to the army, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Ambassador, that we arrested the remaining 5 per cent on several occasions; whenever we found an independent group of that nature, we had it arrested?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that may have happened on one or two occasions. It's also worth bearing in mind that we have had, before this Tribunal, cases of Serb irregulars who committed mayhem and murder and ethnic cleansing. Several of them have been convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal. So that the point you make is perhaps valid in 1 per cent of the cases. I'm just estimating. Perhaps it's 2 per cent. But the reality was that the VRS, aided and abetted by some irregulars, policemen, for example, was carrying out extensive ethnic cleansing during the period you are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I'm going to challenge all of that here, and by way of documents, at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, could this decision, 1D194, be admitted into evidence. And now I would like to ask for 1D -- or, actually, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, you are not obliged to answer, but which one is original, English or the B/C/S, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both were signed on the same day. In English, it was sent to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. But we have a better copy in English. Actually, this was damaged while being up-loaded in e-court. Otherwise, it is more legible when it's not in e-court. It was e-mailed to the relevant service, so it will be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D93, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D205, could I have that document, please. These are congratulations being proffered by myself, the president, on the occasion of the second anniversary of the founding of the party: [In English] "The state, which we the Serbs are creating --" [Interpretation] "The state that we are creating has to be based on the rule of law and humaneness ..." And then we have, under quotation marks, a quotation from the great Serbian poet, [indiscernible]: "A kingdom does not demand inhumane people to defile itself before the world. With that, I ask all members and representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party to constantly monitor our behaviour so that the glory of our just battle would not be tarnished by inhumane actions. Special attention should be given to just behaviour towards civilians of other ethnicities within our republic. Similarly, towards our defeated enemies, we need to not only honour the clauses of the Geneva Convention, we also need to show our Orthodox Christian mercy."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this appeal?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I read it now, and I find it very touching. It's a pity it wasn't not carried out in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It will be shown that it did happen in reality as well. This was published in all media, and, indeed, it did have certain influence. Could it please be admitted? Have we have been assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it Exhibit D94?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D206, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is a telegram, a secret telegram at that, to all presidents of municipalities in the area of Gorazde, because we held half of Gorazde, Foca, Han Pijesak, Sokolac, Rogatica. Now, Visegrad, Rude, Cajnice, Gorazde, Foca, you see, all of that is in the Drina Valley, and this is the text: "All villages in which the Croatian and Muslim inhabitants hand over their weapons and do not intend to fight against us must enjoy the full protection of our Serb state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The responsibility for this must be borne by the presidents of the municipalities." The date is the 14th of July, 1992. Are you aware of the fact that we took such measures as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that on paper, these measures were taken, and I'm also aware, in the video that showed Krajisnik discussing these particular areas, the overlay after your army occupied them showed that numerous municipalities were Muslim, but by the time Krajisnik was showing us that map, between September and December 1992, they were all blue, indicating they were all Serbian. So that is something that has to be taken into account; namely, that these words -- this message that you sent was either not observed by the recipients or perhaps they understood that maybe you didn't really mean every word of it. Because the ethnic cleansing in Foca, for example, was horrific, and several of the Serb cleansers have been tried and convicted here at the International Criminal Tribunal. There is really no argument about that, Dr. Karadzic, unless you wish to accuse the Tribunal of inventing things, and I don't think that's what you want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. As we've already said, and I believe you'll agree with me when I say that everything that came before the "but" is usable, whereas everything after the "but" I reject, when you give your assessments and appraisals of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I'd like to tender this document next, and I'd like to call up 1D30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, along with this document, Mr. Ambassador, you see you spoke tu quoque. This was a secret telegram and order. It was a strict order and calls upon the presidents of the municipality to accountability. And where some municipalities, such as Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica remained Muslim until 1995 and not Serb; isn't that right? Did those municipalities remain Muslim municipalities until 1995, and did the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan and Vance-Owen Plan, did they both envisage them as remaining Muslim municipalities?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gorazde was always seen to be Muslim. Indeed, it was a Muslim area. Today, it is within the federation of Croats and Muslims. It's not in Republika Srpska. Milosevic insisted on that at the very end of the day -- excuse me, he didn't insist on it. The Muslims insisted on it. Since the Serbs had been given their corridor from Belgrade to Banja Luka, through Brcko, they said they should have a corridor to Gorazde, and it was indeed the last night at Dayton when, over a certain amount of whiskey, Milosevic and General Clark and others decided that Gorazde should remain with the Muslim Croat federation. Srebrenica is a similar case up to a point, similar in that both were UN protected areas, safe havens. The UN Security Council and UNPROFOR had declared six cities in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be safe havens; Tuzla, Gorazde, Srebrenica, Bihac -- I don't remember the others. So that as we well know, Srebrenica held many refugees, since it was considered safe. There was a unit of UNPROFOR protecting the city. They were, in fact, Dutch soldiers. And it's also known that in July of 1995, the Bosnian Serb Army, in the presence of General Mladic, and we know that because we have the newspaper -- videos of him addressing his troops, that they murdered 7.000 Bosnian Serb men and boys. Now, if you want to contest that, Dr. Karadzic, I'm fully prepared to enter into a discussion, but I don't think it needs to be argued. It was the most horrific crime during the entire war, and it was the worst single crime of war committed in Europe after World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. My objection remains the same. I reject everything after the "but." And may we have the next document --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does that mean, Dr. Karadzic, that you are denying that Srebrenica occurred -- excuse me for asking, excuse me for interrupting. And I can appreciate that you don't like what I say, but I think in all fairness to the Court, denying the massacre at Srebrenica, I think you owe the Court an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's time to bring the witness to order. I think he's playing a role here that far exceeds his position as a witness. So, please, I think you should ask him to restrict himself to answering the questions, not to making the Prosecution's closing argument or putting questions to Dr. Karadzic. I think it's time for the Chamber to step in and exercise some control over the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ambassador, as you see we have limited time, so please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- be brief in answering the question. Thank you very much. So in the meantime, unless it is objected to, we will admit 1D206.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D95, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 1D300 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Mr. Ambassador, let me inform you that the date is the 23rd of July, my order containing four points, a four-point order. 1D300 is the document number, 1D300: That's it. The English version will suffice. I'll read it in Serbian. So the first conference, the London Conference, is still taking place in London: "Now, on the basis of -- pursuant to the constitutional powers and in keeping with the obligations undertaken at the London Conference, I hereby order: "1. The Serbian authorities must act in accordance with the law and the Geneva Conventions towards the civilian population of any ethnicity who do not exert aggression and combat operations against our army and the civilian population. "2. All the inhabitants who surrender weapons and agree to live peacefully and in keeping with the law must be enabled to remain in their own homes and enjoy our protection." Number 3, and we'll come back to that tomorrow: "Any inhabitants who wish to -- who, from combat operation zones, wish to move temporarily or permanently to other areas must be enabled to do so. The date and route to be used by the population must be agreed upon, and complete security must be provided for the civilians on the move. "4. I hereby warn all representatives of the authorities of the SAO of Birac of their great responsibility before the law to execute this and other orders in keeping with the law and the Geneva Conventions." And the date there is the 23rd of July, 1992. Now, you accuse me of conducting a tu quoque -- tu quoque proceedings, but did you know about this order and orders of this kind? Without the "but" this time, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of this order. I must also state, in connection with Mr. Robinson's point, which I appreciate, that it was not I who raised Srebrenica, it was Dr. Karadzic in his question to me who raised Gorazde and Srebrenica. I was answering his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I just challenged the fact that you said that all the municipalities became blue already in 1992, and we could have stopped there. But I'd like to tender this document into evidence, the order, 1D300.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we have 1D215 called up next, please. Do we have 1D300; is that admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it Exhibit D96?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, Exhibit D96.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now we have the conclusion here, dated the 6th of August, of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it says: "The Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Ministry of Justice," et cetera, "is charged that through its municipal organs of the Interior, in a co-ordinated fashion, collect written information about the relation and conduct of the Serb authorities towards prisoners of war and the conditions of life for prisoners in prisons on the territory of the municipality in which there are such cases -- such prisoners," and then that that be sent to the Presidency within a ten-day dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, did you know that the Presidency made this demand, that it be reported back to and informed about the situation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I'm pleased that you did. It's a pity it wasn't followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will show you that it was -- I will prove that it was, but unfortunately you won't be here then. But I would like you to gain a different impression and picture of the situation while you're here. Now may we have document number 205 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D97, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about 215.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 216 next, please. 1D216 next, please. While we're waiting for that, this was on the same day, a statement of the Presidency on the arrest of renegades. The previous one was the conclusion. Now we're asking for a different one. 215 has been translated. We did have a translation of it and the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This should be the last question for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, the date of this is the 6th of August, 1992. It is a statement from the Presidency on the arrest of renegades: "The Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina informs that several weeks ago, it issued an order whereby all groups and individuals should be placed under the united command of the army and the police. This idea was, for the most part, carried out, except in the case of certain groups of renegades in Podrinje and Kljuc. The Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina arrested groups and individuals who were renegades from the law and who looted and burnt. So it's not a case of the arrest of politically organised individuals or units with other names that were attached to the united command and courageously fighting for the freedom of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina and deserve all commendation." Now, this was issued to quell the people, to show them who we were arresting, who it was we were arresting; that it wasn't combatants who were organised, but that they were renegades. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'd like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect -- no objection with respect to this document and the previous document. There's a translation for both. Both are on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. The 215 was 65 ter 01116. This document is 65 ter 00865, and I think the accompanying translation should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karadzic, we'll adjourn for today, but you have had more than nine hours with Ambassador Okun for your cross-examination, and you originally indicated -- you had asked for fourteen hours. So given that you have approximately -- it would be less than four hours tomorrow, the Chamber expects you to conclude your cross-examination by tomorrow. But I take it that you will have some re-direct, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have for Ambassador Okun, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, it all depends whether we're going to be efficient in asking questions and getting answers. I think that this is a unique occasion, when the Trial Chamber has such a prominent personage before them, who was partly a participant and partly learnt about the situation from other sources. Now, unless the ambassador is adverse to spending more hours in Europe, there could be more -- I would like to have more time, but a minimum of 14 hours, the 14 hours I said to begin with. So if the ambassador agrees, I would like to have more time, because we really do have a lot of documents to get through and to throw light on many more facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the ambassador has been spending more than two weeks already here, so it seems impractical, if not in-humanitarian, to ask him to stay longer. So could you try to finish -- could you try to leave about 20 minutes before the end of tomorrow? Let's see how we go on tomorrow. Tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the number of the last exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D216 will be Exhibit D98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that, we'll adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of April, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
